Hirbidity and Solar Infrared Irradiance over Maitri,Antarctica
Pa van S. Kulkarni*n, S.L. Jain1 , B.C. Aryaf, Sachin D Ghude+ , Ashok Kumar, 
Nazeer Ahammed1  and Shahnawaz*
tRadio and Atmospheric Sciences Division, National Physical Laboratory,

Delhi - 110007 
*Email: pavannpl@yahoo.co.in
ABSTRACT
Aerosol optical depth and solar infrared irradiance at 1020 nm using narrow 
band filter has been measured using a microprocessor based sun photometer during 
1997,2002,2003 and 2004. The observations were taken on hourly basis on all clear 
days at Maitri, an Indian Antarctic Station (70° 46’  S, 11° 45’  fi), during seventeenth, 
twenty first, twenty second and twenty third Indian Scientific Antarctic expedition. 
Very low AOD values and comparatively high solar infrared irradiance at 1020 nm 
have been observed during the entire period of observation at this clean and 
pristine environment of the continent. But found a clear variation in month-to- 
month values of AOD, which can be attributed to the local meteorological conditions.
Keywords: Aerosol optical depth, Solar infrared irradiance, Sun photometer.
INTRODUCTION
Atmospheric aerosol exerts both direct and indirect radiative forcing 
on climate. The attenuation of solar irradiance is mostly due to aerosols and 
Rayleigh scattering. Like other atmospheric constituents aerosols directly 
affects the radiation budget of the atmosphere by the scattering, absorption 
of radiation and shielding the earth against incoming solar radiation. 
Increasing concentrations of aerosols in the atmosphere enhance this effect 
and thereby produce a negative as well as positive radiative forcing. The 
aerosol life time varies from few days to about a week and their concentration 
is highly variable in space and time (Gonzalez et al., 2000). This variable 
aerosol concentration is strongly depend on localized source. It also has a

radiative effect of absorbing and re-emitting long wave infrared radiation. 
The sources of aerosols are both natural and anthropogenic. The most 
effective light-scattering aerosols of natural origin are sulphates formed 
from biogenic gaseous sulphur compounds and organic carbon formed from 
the partial atmospheric oxygen of gaseous biogenic organic compounds. 
Other natural sources include gaseous and particulate emissions from 
volcanoes, wildfire, and desert dust storms. The main anthropogenic source 
of aerosols is gaseous sulphur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen, and carbon 
containing gases. Major light absorbing aerosols are dominated those 
containing black carbon formed from the incomplete combustion of 
carbonaceous fuel. A subset of aerosols (size less than 0.1 im) acts as 
cloud condensation nuclei and thereby affects the cloud formation (Radke 
et al., 1989; Wigley, 1989; Charlson et al., 1992; Coakley et al., 1987). 
Increasing the concentration of these aerosols, indirectly, has the potential 
to change the microphysical, optical, and radiative properties of clouds, which, 
in turn, can change their reflective and absorbance properties and 
persistence. Aerosols play an important role in the heterogeneous chemistry 
and thereby in the tropical stratospheric ozone (Hofmann and Solomon, 
1989) through providing surfaces for condensation and heterogeneous 
chemistry.
The vast ice sheet of Antarctica, is located in the southern hemisphere 
with no or very little human activity and has only about 2% bare land area 
exposed to the atmosphere (Deshpande and Kamra, 2000). The air is 
generally pristine and is only influenced by the long range transport of sub- 
micro-size particles and gaseous pollutants (Gadhavi and Jayaraman, 2004). 
Thus Antarctic region is an unique location for the background measurement 
of AOD due to the absence of any major local aerosol source and it’s clean 
environment. Aerosol studies over the sites such as Antarctica will help in 
estimating the background level aerosol forcing over a pristine site. Factors 
like high surface albedo and unique solar insolation cycle over Antarctica 
also makes the study an interesting one.
Aerosol optical depth describes aerosol effects on radiative transfer. 
It is a column integrated measurement of the relative extinction of direct 
sunlight due to aerosol scattering and is defined by means of the Bouguer- 
Lambert law. The spectral aerosol optical depth is also known as turbidity. 
The monitoring of aerosol optical thickness or turbidity is an important 
parameter for studying global climatic change. Sun photometers have widely 
been used to measure aerosol optical thickness and other properties of the 
atmosphere (Volz, 1974; Flowers, 1969; Shaw, 1983; King and Byrne,
